claim: Paraformaldehyde (PFA) is one of the most commonly used fixatives to create covalent cross-linking between biomolecules.
source: Due to its small size and high reactivity with a wide range of biological entities, paraformaldehyde (PFA) is one of the most commonly used fixatives to create covalent cross-linking between biomolecules, for example, proteins and nucleic acids.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of cell biology and is stated directly in the manuscript.

claim: PFA nonselectively fixes or cross-links molecules in proximity to enable characterization of biomolecular interactions formed in living cells.
source: PFA nonselectively 'fixes' or cross-links molecules in proximity to enable characterization of biomolecular interactions formed in living cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the mechanism and purpose of PFA fixation.

claim: Transcription factors bound to DNA with fast dissociation dynamics (<5 s residence times) are not cross-linked to DNA upon PFA fixation.
source: By imaging different transcription factors (TFs) in live and fixed cells, Schmiedeberg et al., 2009 showed that TFs bound to DNA with fast dissociation dynamics (<5 s residence times as determined by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching [FRAP]) are not cross-linked to DNA upon PFA fixation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schmiedeberg et al., 2009.

claim: Transcription factors stay bound to chromosome during mitosis and fixing cells can artificially deplete transiently bound TFs from mitotic chromosomes.
source: Using live-cell single-molecule imaging, Teves et al., 2016 showed that TFs stay bound to chromosome during mitosis and fixing cells can artificially deplete transiently bound TFs from mitotic chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Teves et al., 2016.

claim: The efficiency and rates at which PFA reacts with proteins can vary by orders of magnitude.
source: For example, the efficiency and rates at which PFA reacts with proteins can vary by orders of magnitude (Kamps et al., 2019) and are dependent on their amino acid sequences (Kamps et al., 2019; Metz et al., 2004; Sutherland et al., 2008) and tertiary structures (Hoffman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Kamps et al., 2019; Metz et al., 2004; Sutherland et al., 2008; Hoffman et al., 2015).

claim: LLPS is driven by excessive levels of transient, selective, and multivalent protein–protein interactions mediated by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).
source: LLPS is driven by excessive levels of transient, selective, and multivalent protein–protein interactions mediated by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) within the proteins of interest (Chong et al., 2018; Kato and McKnight, 2018; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chong et al., 2018; Kato and McKnight, 2018; Li et al., 2012.

claim: Detection of discrete puncta that have a spherical shape, undergo fusion and fission, and dynamically exchange biomolecules with the surrounding according to FRAP is often considered evidence of putative LLPS in living cells.
source: Whereas rigorous characterization of LLPS in vivo has been challenging and remains a question under active investigation (McSwiggen et al., 2019b), detection of discrete puncta that have a spherical shape, undergo fusion and fission, and dynamically exchange biomolecules with the surrounding according to FRAP is often considered evidence of putative LLPS in living cells.
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in the field, with a citation to McSwiggen et al., 2019b regarding the challenges of characterization.

claim: Detecting local high-concentration regions or puncta of an endogenously expressed protein using immunofluorescence of fixed cells has been used in many studies as evidence of LLPS.
source: Detecting local high-concentration regions or puncta of an endogenously expressed protein using immunofluorescence of fixed cells has been used in many studies as evidence of LLPS (Boija et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2019; Owen et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Boija et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2019; Owen et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2020).

claim: PFA fixation enhances the appearance of LLPS for FET family protein IDRs (FUS, EWS, and TAF15).
source: Interestingly, after fixation, the puncta of all three IDRs appear to increase in their numbers, sizes, and contrast compared with the dilute phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and quantified in Figure 1D-F.

claim: PFA fixation can artificially turn a cell with EGFP-EWS(IDR) homogeneously distributed in the nucleus without any puncta into one with many discrete puncta.
source: In particular, PFA fixation was able to artificially turn a cell with EGFP-EWS(IDR) homogeneously distributed in the nucleus without any puncta into one with many discrete puncta (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: After fixation, the number of puncta, surface roughness, and punctate percentage of EGFP-EWS(IDR), EGFP-FUS(IDR), and EGFP-TAF15(IDR) significantly increase.
source: We quantified the fixation-induced changes of LLPS appearance by calculating three parameters from the fluorescence images of cells, including the number of puncta, surface roughness, and punctate percentage, and found a significant increase in all three parameters after fixation (Figure 1D–F, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Fixation is complete in approximately 100 seconds.
source: We performed real-time imaging of live cells expressing EGFP-FUS(IDR) and found that their morphology and LLPS appearance start to change immediately upon PFA treatment and reach a steady state after ~100 s of treatment (Video 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Video 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Statistically significant changes to LLPS-describing parameters occur upon fixation at PFA concentrations of 1, 2, 4, and 8%.
source: We treated cells expressing EGFP-EWS(IDR) with different concentrations of PFA (1, 2, 4, and 8%) and observed statistically significant changes to the above three LLPS-describing parameters upon fixation at all the concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Statistically significant fixation-induced changes to the apparent LLPS behavior of EGFP-EWS(IDR) occur using 4% PFA and 0.2% GA in combination.
source: However, we still observed statistically significant fixation-induced changes to the apparent LLPS behavior of EGFP-EWS(IDR) using 4% PFA and 0.2% GA in combination (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: DsRed2-TAF15(IDR) shows enhanced LLPS behavior upon fixation with thousands of smaller puncta emerging in the dilute phase.
source: The LLPS behavior of DsRed2-TAF15(IDR) is enhanced upon fixation like EGFP-TAF15(IDR) (Figure 2A), but the enhancement has a different appearance. Whereas there is not a significant change to the large preformed DsRed2-TAF15(IDR) puncta, thousands of smaller puncta emerge in the dilute phase within the nucleus (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Halo-TAF15(IDR) displays diminished LLPS behavior after fixation, with puncta becoming smaller and dimmer or completely disappearing.
source: In contrast, Halo-TAF15(IDR) displays a diminished LLPS behavior after fixation, with its puncta becoming smaller and dimmer or completely disappearing (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: EGFP-FUS(FL) overexpressed in live U2OS cells forms many small puncta throughout the nucleus, and this behavior does not significantly change after PFA fixation.
source: We found that EGFP-FUS(FL) overexpressed in live U2OS cells forms many small puncta throughout the nucleus, and we did not observe a significant change of this behavior after PFA fixation (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TAF15(IDR)-Halo-FTH1 overexpressed in live U2OS cells forms large droplet-like puncta and the appearance of LLPS does not significantly change after PFA fixation.
source: We found that TAF15(IDR)-Halo-FTH1 overexpressed in live U2OS cells forms large droplet-like puncta and the appearance of LLPS does not significantly change after PFA fixation (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The distribution of endogenous EWS::FLI1-Halo in A673 cells does not significantly change after PFA fixation.
source: Here, we compared live and fixed A673 cell images of endogenous EWS::FLI1-Halo and did not observe a significant difference in its distribution (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Adding 25 mM glycine to live U2OS cells that overexpress DsRed2-TAF15(IDR) increases the starting punctate percentage from 18 ± 1.92 to 36 ± 3.82%.
source: We found that adding 25 mM glycine to live U2OS cells that overexpress DsRed2-TAF15(IDR) increases the starting punctate percentage from 18 ± 1.92 to 36 ± 3.82% (quantified from 23 cells), indicating an increase in the degree of LLPS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data quantified from 23 cells.

claim: Addition of glycine dramatically reverses the fixation effect on the LLPS behavior of DsRed2-TAF15(IDR).
source: Importantly, addition of glycine dramatically reversed the fixation effect on the LLPS behavior of DsRed2-TAF15(IDR). Whereas PFA fixation in the absence of additional glycine enhances the LLPS appearance (Figure 2B, Figure 4A), in the presence of 25 mM glycine, fixation causes many of the smaller puncta formed in live cells to disappear completely and larger, preformed puncta to turn into a 'donut' shape, with the outline of the puncta still visible but the interior devoid of the protein (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, Figure 4A, and Figure 4B.

claim: When the fixation rate is the same in and out of puncta (k3=k4), the live-cell equilibrium is perfectly preserved in fixed cells regardless of the starting punctate percentage.
source: In the scenario where the rate of fixation is the same in and out of the puncta (k3=k4), the live-cell equilibrium is perfectly preserved in fixed cells regardless of the starting punctate percentage (ΔPunctate Percentage~0).
evidence: This claim is based on simulation results from the kinetic model.

claim: When the fixation rate inside the puncta is greater than outside the puncta (k3 > k4), the fixed cell will have a higher punctate percentage than the live cell.
source: When the fixation rate inside the puncta is greater than outside the puncta (k3 > k4), the fixed cell will have a higher punctate percentage than the live cell, that is, fixation enhances the apparent LLPS behaviors.
evidence: This claim is based on simulation results from the kinetic model.

claim: When the fixation rate outside the puncta is greater than inside the puncta (k4>k3), the fixed cells will have diminished apparent LLPS behaviors than in the live cell.
source: When the balance is reversed (k4>k3), the fixed cells will have diminished apparent LLPS behaviors than in the live cell.
evidence: This claim is based on simulation results from the kinetic model.

claim: When protein–protein interactions are highly dynamic compared with the overall fixation rates ((k3+k4)≪(k1+k2)), the fixation artifact is the most pronounced.
source: We found when the protein–protein interactions are highly dynamic compared with the overall fixation rates ((k3+k4)≪(k1+k2)), the fixation artifact is the most pronounced as shown by a large value of ΔPunctate Percentage.
evidence: This claim is based on simulation results from the kinetic model.

claim: When protein–protein interactions are stable and less dynamic compared with the overall fixation rate ((k3+k4)≫(k1+k2)), there is a minimal fixation artifact.
source: In contrast, when the protein–protein interactions are stable and less dynamic compared with the overall fixation rate ((k3+k4)≫(k1+k2)), there is a minimal fixation artifact and the punctate percentage in fixed cells is similar to that in living cells (ΔPunctate Percentage ~ 0).
evidence: This claim is based on simulation results from the kinetic model.

claim: Different fixation rates of POI in and out of puncta (k3:k4≠1:1) are required for fixation artifacts to happen.
source: Different fixation rates of POI in and out of puncta (k3:k4≠1:1) are required for fixation artifacts to happen and the value of k3:k4 determines whether the LLPS behavior of POI gets over-represented or under-represented in fixed cell images.
evidence: This claim is based on simulation results from the kinetic model.

claim: The residence time of TAF15(IDR) at droplet-like puncta is 10.23 ± 1.10 s.
source: Using established single-particle tracking (SPT) analysis (Chong et al., 2018), we found the RTs of TAF15(IDR) and TAF15(IDR)-FTH1 to be 10.23 ± 1.10 and 64.15 ± 11.65 s, respectively (Figure 6, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-particle tracking shown in Figure 6.

claim: The residence time of TAF15(IDR)-FTH1 at droplet-like puncta is 64.15 ± 11.65 s.
source: Using established single-particle tracking (SPT) analysis (Chong et al., 2018), we found the RTs of TAF15(IDR) and TAF15(IDR)-FTH1 to be 10.23 ± 1.10 and 64.15 ± 11.65 s, respectively (Figure 6, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-particle tracking shown in Figure 6.

claim: TAF15(IDR)-FTH1 has significantly more stable binding than TAF15(IDR).
source: This result suggests significantly more stable binding of TAF15(IDR)-FTH1 than TAF15(IDR).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the residence time measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: A fast overall fixation rate relative to binding dynamics can minimize fixation artifacts.
source: Together, these imaging data are consistent with our model's prediction that a fast overall fixation rate relative to binding dynamics can minimize fixation artifacts.
evidence: This claim is supported by both simulation results and experimental data comparing TAF15(IDR) and TAF15(IDR)-FTH1.

claim: Fixation can change the appearance of phase separation in living cells.
source: For the first time, our work reveals an important caveat in using fixation-based methods to detect and characterize LLPS in vivo and suggests an advantage of using live-cell imaging to study LLPS systems over fixed-cell experiments.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental observations.

claim: Fixation-induced changes of LLPS appearance may lead to potential misinterpretation of the functional relevance of LLPS in cellular processes.
source: We note that fixation-induced changes of LLPS appearance may lead to potential misinterpretation of the functional relevance of LLPS in cellular processes.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications of the findings.

claim: The dynamics of POI binding to and dissociating from puncta, the absolute fixation rate of POI, and different fixation rates of POI in and out of puncta all play a role in inducing fixation artifacts.
source: To understand the factors that can cause fixation-induced changes of LLPS appearance in the cell, we simulated the changes through kinetic modeling, which reveals that the dynamics of POI binding to and dissociating from puncta, the absolute fixation rate of POI, and different fixation rates of POI in and out of puncta all play a role in inducing the fixation artifacts.
evidence: This claim is based on simulation results from the kinetic model.

claim: The logical implications of the four-state model can extend beyond LLPS to other biomolecular transactions and cellular structures.
source: We emphasize that because our four-state model makes no assumptions about any state being phase-separated, the logical implications of our model can extend beyond LLPS to other biomolecular transactions and cellular structures that have been found not well preserved by fixation or immunofluorescence, including localizations of cilia proteins (Hua and Ferland, 2017), clustering of cell membrane receptors (Stanly et al., 2016), splicing speckle formation (Neugebauer and Roth, 1997), and chromatin organization and protein binding (Zarębski et al., 2021; Lorber and Volk, 2022; Lerner et al., 2016; Pallier et al., 2003; Kumar et al., 2008 and Teves et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the broader applicability of the model, supported by citations to other studies.

claim: Fixation artifacts will occur whenever a protein can exist in multiple states that have different rates of fixation, and this artifact is most severe when the fixation is slower than the transition between states.
source: Generally, our model predicts that fixation artifacts will occur whenever a protein can exist in multiple states that have different rates of fixation, and this artifact is most severe when the fixation is slower than the transition between states.
evidence: This is a general prediction based on the kinetic model.

claim: Fixing the bound state of an LLPS system (within puncta) is dominated by cross-linking reactions between IDRs enriched in puncta, which have reactive residues better exposed to solvent due to lack of well-defined tertiary structures.
source: We hypothesize that this is because fixing the bound state of an LLPS system (within puncta) is dominated by cross-linking reactions between IDRs enriched in puncta, which have reactive residues better exposed to solvent due to lack of well-defined tertiary structures and thereby likely cross-link faster than structured domains cross-linking to DNA (Hoffman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed differences, with a citation to Hoffman et al., 2015.

claim: FET family protein IDRs (AA2-214 of FUS, AA47-266 of EWS, and AA2-205 of TAF15) are reported to undergo putative LLPS in cells upon overexpression.
source: We focused on the FET family protein IDRs (AA2-214 of FUS, AA47-266 of EWS, and AA2-205 of TAF15) that are reported to undergo putative LLPS in cells upon overexpression (Altmeyer et al., 2015; Chong et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Altmeyer et al., 2015; Chong et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018.

claim: At high enough expression levels, all three FET family IDRs are able to form discrete and spherical puncta in the live cell nucleus, which show fusion and fission behaviors.
source: At high enough expression levels, all three IDRs are able to form discrete and spherical puncta in the live cell nucleus, which show fusion and fission behaviors and are thereby consistent with LLPS droplets (Alberti et al., 2019; Banani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and citations to Alberti et al., 2019; Banani et al., 2017.

claim: Full-length FUS is reported to have a greater LLPS propensity in vitro than its IDR alone.
source: Full-length FUS is reported to have a greater LLPS propensity in vitro than its IDR alone (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: EWS::FLI1 is an oncogenic transcription factor causing Ewing sarcoma.
source: In addition, we looked into a native IDR-containing protein, EWS::FLI1, an oncogenic TF causing Ewing sarcoma (Grünewald et al., 2018) and known to form local high-concentration hubs at target genes associated with GGAA microsatellites (Chong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grünewald et al., 2018 and Chong et al., 2018.

claim: EWS::FLI1 is known to form local high-concentration hubs at target genes associated with GGAA microsatellites.
source: In addition, we looked into a native IDR-containing protein, EWS::FLI1, an oncogenic TF causing Ewing sarcoma (Grünewald et al., 2018) and known to form local high-concentration hubs at target genes associated with GGAA microsatellites (Chong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chong et al., 2018.

claim: Glycine is highly reactive with formaldehyde and is commonly used to quench the formation of protein–protein cross-linked complexes.
source: Glycine is highly reactive with formaldehyde and is commonly used to quench the formation of protein–protein cross-linked complexes by quickly forming protein–glycine and glycine–glycine cross-linked adducts instead (Hoffman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hoffman et al., 2015.

claim: The dilute and concentrated phases of an LLPS system have different protein composition and concentrations.
source: It is well-established that the dilute and concentrated phases of an LLPS system have different protein composition and concentrations (Currie and Rosen, 2022; Koga et al., 2011; Nott et al., 2015; Yewdall et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Currie and Rosen, 2022; Koga et al., 2011; Nott et al., 2015; Yewdall et al., 2021.

claim: The timescale of fixation ranges from seconds to hours.
source: The rate of fixation is known to vary with both factors by orders of magnitude, with the timescale of fixation ranging from seconds to hours (Hoffman et al., 2015; Kamps et al., 2019; Metz et al., 2006; Metz et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hoffman et al., 2015; Kamps et al., 2019; Metz et al., 2006; Metz et al., 2004.

claim: Protein–protein interactions that drive LLPS are highly dynamic with binding residence times in the range of seconds to tens of seconds.
source: Because protein–protein interactions that drive LLPS are highly dynamic with binding residence times in the range of seconds to tens of seconds (Chong et al., 2018), fixation likely happens with either lower or comparable rates than protein binding and dissociation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chong et al., 2018.

claim: Effective transcriptional activation requires an optimum of TF IDR-IDR interactions within TF hubs formed at target genes.
source: For example, recent work has uncovered that effective transcriptional activation requires an optimum of TF IDR-IDR interactions within TF hubs formed at target genes and that overly high levels of IDR-IDR interactions pushing the system toward LLPS can repress transcription (Chong et al., 2022; Trojanowski et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chong et al., 2022; Trojanowski et al., 2022.

claim: Live-imaging techniques that allow estimation of protein diffusion coefficients within specific cellular compartments can be useful alternative approaches for diagnosing LLPS in vivo without the potential artifact of fixation.
source: Live-imaging techniques that allow estimation of protein diffusion coefficients within specific cellular compartments, for example, SPT (Hansen et al., 2018; Heckert et al., 2022) and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (Lanzanò et al., 2017), can be useful alternative approaches for diagnosing LLPS in vivo without the potential artifact of fixation, as diffusion dynamics are recently shown to be affected by LLPS (Heltberg et al., 2021; McSwiggen et al., 2019a; Miné-Hattab et al., 2021; Chong et al., 2022; Ladouceur et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Hansen et al., 2018; Heckert et al., 2022; Lanzanò et al., 2017; Heltberg et al., 2021; McSwiggen et al., 2019a; Miné-Hattab et al., 2021; Chong et al., 2022; Ladouceur et al., 2020).

claim: Diffusion dynamics are recently shown to be affected by LLPS.
source: Live-imaging techniques that allow estimation of protein diffusion coefficients within specific cellular compartments, for example, SPT (Hansen et al., 2018; Heckert et al., 2022) and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (Lanzanò et al., 2017), can be useful alternative approaches for diagnosing LLPS in vivo without the potential artifact of fixation, as diffusion dynamics are recently shown to be affected by LLPS (Heltberg et al., 2021; McSwiggen et al., 2019a; Miné-Hattab et al., 2021; Chong et al., 2022; Ladouceur et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heltberg et al., 2021; McSwiggen et al., 2019a; Miné-Hattab et al., 2021; Chong et al., 2022; Ladouceur et al., 2020.

claim: PFA fixation has been used to faithfully preserve live-cell conditions in many scenarios.
source: Although PFA fixation has been used to faithfully preserve live-cell conditions in many scenarios, a number of studies have uncovered situations in which fixation fails to cross-link DNA–protein interactions formed in living cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the general use of PFA fixation in the field.

claim: Fixation, with limited reaction rates, cannot provide an instantaneous snapshot and may miss or obfuscate biomolecular interactions that happen either at or faster than the timescale of fixation.
source: These studies exemplify the fact that fixation, with limited reaction rates, cannot provide an instantaneous snapshot and may miss or obfuscate biomolecular interactions that happen either at or faster than the timescale of fixation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies about fixation limitations.

claim: The reactivity and reaction rates of PFA are variable and dependent on its biomolecule substrates.
source: What further complicates the result of cell fixation is that the reactivity and reaction rates of PFA are variable and dependent on its biomolecule substrates (Gavrilov et al., 2015; Shishodia et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gavrilov et al., 2015; Shishodia et al., 2018.

claim: Normal DMEM media already contains 0.4 mM glycine.
source: It should be noted that normal DMEM media already contains 0.4 mM glycine.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the composition of DMEM media.

claim: The U2OS cell line used was validated by whole-genome sequencing.
source: The U2OS cell line used here was validated by whole-genome sequencing as described in Hansen et al., 2017.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hansen et al., 2017.

claim: The knock-in A673 cell line was generated by genome editing of the A673 cell line that was comprehensively authenticated by ATCC before distribution.
source: The knock-in A673 cell line was generated by genome editing of the A673 cell line that was comprehensively authenticated by ATCC before distribution (ATCC, CRL-1598).
evidence: This is a statement about the source and authentication of the cell line.

claim: The knock-in A673 cell line showed a 100% match with A673 in STR profiling.
source: The knock-in A673 cell line was further authenticated using Short Tandem Repeat (STR) profiling (ATCC Cell Line Authentication Service) against the following loci: TH01, D5S818, D13S317, D7S820, D16S539, CSF1PO, Amelogenin, vWA, and TPOX. The knock-in A673 cell line showed a 100% match with A673.
evidence: This is experimental data about cell line authentication.

claim: Both U2OS and A673 cell lines were tested for mycoplasma using PCR-based assays in February 2022.
source: Both U2OS and A673 cell lines were tested for mycoplasma using PCR-based assays in February 2022.
evidence: This is a statement about quality control procedures.
